claims.text: Elemental Cr coatings on zirconium-alloy cladding are prone to Cr–Zr interdiffusion at elevated temperatures.
Nitrogen-rich plasma treatment at 400–500 °C for 30–60 minutes will form a CrN surface layer on the elemental Cr coating.
In-situ stress monitoring can be used to minimize residual stress during CrN-layer formation.
The nitriding treatment will produce a dense, uniform, and well-adherent CrN layer.
A zone of metallic Cr will remain beneath the CrN layer and bonded to the zirconium alloy.
The CrN layer will impede oxygen ingress at high temperature.
The CrN layer will suppress interdiffusion between Cr and Zr.
The underlying metallic Cr will retain ductility and thermal-shock resistance.
The combination of a nitrided surface and underlying metallic Cr will protect the cladding in both low-temperature water and high-temperature steam.
Plasma-nitrided Cr coatings will have lower oxidation rates than unmodified Cr coatings.
Plasma-nitrided Cr coatings will exhibit less Cr–Zr interdiffusion than unmodified Cr coatings.
Plasma-nitrided Cr coatings will retain better coating integrity than unmodified Cr coatings.
The proposed treatment will extend cladding service life under dual-environment conditions.
The unmodified elemental Cr coating performs acceptably in either subcritical water or high-temperature steam but fails when both conditions are encountered because of oxidation and interdiffusion.
A static autoclave exposure at 320 °C and 11.3 MPa for 20–60 days is an established aqueous corrosion-test protocol.
Accident-relevant performance is to be evaluated in steam at approximately 1200 °C for 1–2 hours.
CrN is sufficiently inert to justify assuming stability under extreme radiation and nuclear-environment conditions.

contradictions.description: The stated subcritical-water performance boundary is 15–30 days, whereas the proposed falsification experiment includes exposures of 20–60 days, extending beyond that declared boundary.
